note: Winter on Tibetan plateau; roads closed by snow. Lipulekh Pass impassable.
skip_reason: Extreme cold (−20 to −30°C), heavy snow, pass closure, altitude risk.
why_not: The Lipulekh Pass and approach roads are blocked by deep snow. Temperatures plummet to −20 to −30°C on the plateau. Acclimatization becomes nearly impossible; altitude sickness and frostbite are acute risks. The yatra does not operate in winter.

note: Lipulekh Pass and Tibetan roads remain closed. Extreme altitude and cold persist.
skip_reason: Pass blocked, extreme cold (−15 to −25°C), zero government yatra operations.
why_not: Late winter conditions persist. The pass remains impassable. Even if roads clear, acclimatization time is insufficient and medical support is non-existent. The Indian government does not permit yatra operations in winter due to safety protocols.

note: Lipulekh Pass clearing, but still risky. Spring snows unpredictable. Yatra prep begins.
skip_reason: Pass unstable, avalanche risk, roads not fully open, permit allocation starts in May.
why_not: Spring avalanche risk is acute. The pass is partially open but unstable. Government permits are not issued until May. Yatra logistics are not deployed. Early arrivals face long delays, extreme weather swings, and limited support.

note: Pass opens mid-month, but yatra does not commence until May. Weather unpredictable.
skip_reason: Yatra operations not yet active, spring storms, reduced support infrastructure.
why_not: Though the pass becomes passable by late April, government yatra operations do not begin until May. Early independent attempts face unsupported conditions, unpredictable weather, and insufficient acclimatization logistics.

note: Peak yatra window. Clear skies, stable weather, full government support, permit allocation in full swing.
why_go: May is the official start of the yatra season. The Lipulekh Pass is open, skies are predominantly clear, and air temperatures at base (−5 to 5°C) support acclimatization. Government permits are being allocated. The 52 km Kailash Parikrama is fully accessible, and the sacred Mansarovar Lake pilgrimage defines the spiritual journey. Dolma La at 5,630m is navigable, though technical.

note: Peak season continues. Weather most stable. Shortest acclimatization time. High permit competition.
why_go: June offers the most stable weather window of the season. Daytime temperatures can briefly reach 10–15°C at lower elevations. The Kailash Parikrama is fully accessible. Acclimatization windows are tight but manageable for fit pilgrims. Permits are being actively allocated. This is the safest large-group window.

note: Monsoon arrives. Clouds, heavy rain at lower elevations, road damage. Yatra closed.
skip_reason: Monsoon rains damage roads, increased landslide risk, cloud cover, yatra season officially ends.
why_not: July marks the onset of the Southwest Monsoon. Roads on the Indian side and in Tibet become unstable due to heavy rain and landslides. Cloud cover obscures passes and peaks. The Indian government officially closes yatra operations by mid-July. Acclimatization becomes dangerous; altitude sickness risk spikes.

note: Monsoon transitioning. Some clear windows. Permits still available but diminishing. Lower crowds.
why_go: August is a marginal window as monsoon breaks clear. Occasional multi-day windows of clear skies occur. Temperatures are milder (5–10°C daytime). Permit competition drops. Experienced trekkers can find good conditions if flexible. The Parikrama route is still accessible, though weather windows are unpredictable.

note: Post-monsoon clarity. Second peak season window. Stable weather returns. Permits actively issued.
why_go: September marks the return of stable post-monsoon skies. Clear visibility returns; daytime temperatures remain mild (5–15°C). The Lipulekh Pass is wide open. The Kailash Parikrama is fully navigable, and Mansarovar Lake is ice-free. This is the secondary peak season; permits are actively issued, and conditions rival May–June.

note: Yatra season closing. Early snow on passes. Permits being wound down. Risky window.
skip_reason: Season officially ending, early snow, reduced support, acclimatization windows narrow.
why_not: October marks the close of the yatra season. Early snow falls on the higher passes. Permits are being discontinued. Government support infrastructure is being withdrawn. Weather becomes unstable; temperatures drop to −5 to 0°C. Acclimatization becomes risky. Only the hardiest expeditions attempt this window, and government policy discourages it.

note: Winter arrives. Lipulekh Pass closing. No permits issued. Extreme cold begins.
skip_reason: Pass closing, winter onset, no government support, temperature −10 to −20°C.
why_not: November brings the onset of winter. Snow accumulates on passes and roads. The Lipulekh Pass begins closing toward month-end. The Indian government officially ends yatra operations. Temperatures plummet to −10 to −20°C. Acclimatization support is withdrawn. This is categorically unsafe for pilgrims.

note: Winter fully established. Roads and pass closed. Coldest month. No access possible.
skip_reason: Complete road closure, extreme cold (−20 to −30°C), zero government support.
why_not: December is the deepest part of winter. The Lipulekh Pass is completely closed by snow. Roads are impassable. Temperatures range from −20 to −30°C on the Tibetan plateau. Acclimatization is impossible; frostbite and hypothermia are immediate threats. No government support exists. This window is absolutely unsafe.

note: Winter snow on high passes. Road to Dharchula is accessible but mountain passes are blocked.
skip_reason: High passes closed by snow, extreme cold, altitude risk, Inner Line Permit still required.
why_not: Winter conditions prevail. The routes to Jolingkong Lake and Om Parvat are blocked by snow above 3,500m. Temperatures drop to −10 to −15°C at base. The Inner Line Permit is still required but roads toward the border become risky. Acclimatization is dangerous; medical support is limited.

note: Winter persists. Snow on all high passes. Coldest month with limited road access.
skip_reason: Deep snow on passes, extreme cold (−15 to −20°C), minimal support infrastructure.
why_not: February is the coldest month. All high passes toward Chhota Kailash (Om Parvat route) are buried in snow. The Om Parvat snowfield is too unstable for safe trekking. Temperatures at Dharchula hover around −10°C, making acclimatization and sleeping-bag management risky. Limited trekking infrastructure is available.

note: Spring snow melt begins. Avalanche risk. Passes clearing but unstable. Early permit season.
skip_reason: Avalanche risk from snow melt, pass instability, spring snow squalls unpredictable.
why_not: March brings spring snow melt, triggering avalanche hazards on high routes. The Om Parvat slopes are unstable. Dharchula temperatures warm to 0–5°C but higher elevations remain treacherous. Permit offices open but infrastructure is minimal. Early trekkers face unpredictable weather and limited support.

note: Spring in full swing. Passes opening. Clear skies frequent. Permit processing active. Good shoulder season.
things_to_do: Dharchula town and Inner Line Permit office
why_go: April marks the true spring opening. Passes are open and stable. The Om Parvat snowfield holds the sacred white Om symbol. Temperatures are mild (5–15°C daytime). Clear skies dominate. The Inner Line Permit is easily obtained from Dharchula SDM office (1–3 days). This is an excellent shoulder season for pilgrims and trekkers seeking solitude and excellent views.

note: Peak season. Clear weather, all routes open. Popular pilgrimage window. Full support.
why_go: May is prime season. Skies are consistently clear; daytime temperatures are warm (15–20°C). All passes are fully open. The Om Parvat snowfield displays the sacred symbol clearly. Jolingkong Lake is accessible without snow obstacles. The Inner Line Permit is quickly obtained. Infrastructure (lodges, guides) is fully operational. This is the most crowded but safest window.

note: Peak continues. Weather stable. Monsoon not yet arrived. Lush green landscapes.
why_go: June extends the peak season. Temperatures are warm (10–18°C). The landscape greens; wildflowers bloom on lower slopes. The monsoon has not yet arrived; skies remain clear. Jolingkong Lake is fully thawed and accessible for ritual bathing. This is a secondary peak window with excellent visibility and comfortable hiking conditions.

note: Early monsoon. Heavy rains at lower elevations. Cloud cover. Trails become slippery.
skip_reason: Monsoon rains, landslide risk on trekking trails, cloud cover obscures views.
why_not: July brings the full Southwest Monsoon. Heavy rains drench the region below 4,000m. Trails become muddy and slippery; landslide risk is acute on the approach to Dharchula and toward Jolingkong Lake. Cloud cover obscures Om Parvat and surrounding peaks. The Inner Line Permit office may face reduced hours due to weather.

note: Monsoon transitioning. Some clear windows. Higher passes accessible. Reduced crowds.
why_not: August straddles monsoon and post-monsoon. Occasional clear windows occur, but rain is still common. Lower elevations remain wet. The trek to Jolingkong Lake is passable but muddy. Daytime temperatures are mild (8–15°C). If you find a multi-day clear window, the trek is feasible, but planning flexibility is required.

note: Post-monsoon clarity returns. Second peak season. Stable weather. Clear skies dominant.
why_go: September is the secondary peak season. Post-monsoon clouds clear; skies are predominantly clear. Temperatures are mild (8–18°C daytime). Visibility of Om Parvat and Chhota Kailash is excellent. Trails dry out. The Inner Line Permit is still easily obtained. Infrastructure remains fully operational. Crowds are lower than May–June, making this an excellent choice.

note: Autumn clarity. Cooler temperatures. Reduced monsoon risk. Good shoulder season.
who_should_avoid: Those uncomfortable with rapidly cooling nights
why_go: October brings autumn clarity and cooler daytime temperatures (5–15°C). Frost appears at higher elevations but does not block passes. The Om Parvat snowfield is pristine. Trails are dry. The Inner Line Permit process remains straightforward. This is a beautiful shoulder season with fewer trekkers and excellent conditions.

note: Early winter. First snow on high passes. Temperatures dropping. Permit offices reducing hours.
skip_reason: Early snow on high passes, rapid temperature drop, reduced infrastructure support.
why_not: November marks the transition to winter. Early snows close higher passes above 4,500m. Temperatures drop to −5 to 0°C at altitude. The Dharchula Inner Line Permit office may reduce hours. Acclimatization becomes risky as daytime warmth decreases. This is an unsafe window for most trekkers.

note: Winter established. High passes closed. Extreme cold. Roads may face closures.
skip_reason: High passes blocked by snow, extreme cold (−15 to −20°C), minimal support.
why_not: December is deep winter. All passes above 4,500m are closed by snow. Temperatures plummet to −15 to −20°C. Road conditions toward the border become hazardous. The Inner Line Permit office operates minimally. Acclimatization and altitude sickness are major risks. This window is unsafe.

note: Deep winter. All high routes closed by snow. Temperatures −20°C at altitude.
skip_reason: All high passes and trekking routes closed by deep snow, extreme cold, zero support.
why_not: January is severe winter. The Kinner Kailash Parikrama route at 4,800–6,055m is completely snowbound. Temperatures drop to −20°C or lower. Avalanche danger is extreme. No pilgrims trek in this month. The base village Kalpa is accessible by road but the trek is categorically impossible.

note: Winter deep. Snow cover complete. Extreme cold persists. No access routes open.
skip_reason: Complete snow closure, extreme cold (−15 to −20°C), avalanche risk at maximum.
why_not: February is the coldest month. All trekking routes are buried under snow. The Shivling rock formation at 4,800m is inaccessible. Kalpa town is accessible but remains extremely cold (−10 to −5°C). No trekking is possible. This window is absolutely unsafe.

note: Spring snow melt. Avalanche hazards peak. Passes unstable. Routes still blocked.
skip_reason: Avalanche risk from melt, pass instability, snow depth still prohibitive.
why_not: March brings spring snow melt and high avalanche risk on all high slopes. The Parikrama route remains snow-choked. Kalpa is accessible by road but temperatures still drop to −5 to 0°C at night. Trekking routes are unstable and impassable.

note: Spring progression. Snow clearing from lower elevations. Kalpa accessible by road.
skip_reason: High routes still snow-covered, late-season avalanche risk, full trek not yet viable.
why_not: April brings spring warmth to lower elevations. Kalpa is fully accessible by road; daytime temperatures reach 10–15°C. However, the higher Parikrama route (above 4,800m) remains snow-covered. The trek is not fully open until June. This is an early planning window but not for trekking.

note: Late spring. Snow clearing but higher passes still blocked. Full trek not yet open.
skip_reason: Upper Parikrama route still snow-covered, pass accessibility questionable, summer not yet started.
why_not: May sees continued snow clearing at mid-elevations, but the core Parikrama circuit above 5,000m is still heavily snow-covered. Temperatures at Kalpa are warm (15–20°C), but higher elevations remain treacherous. The full trek does not fully open until early June.

note: Peak season opens. High routes accessible. Clear skies dominant. All trekking viable.
why_go: June marks the official opening of the Kinner Kailash season. All high routes are accessible. Daytime temperatures are mild (5–15°C). Clear skies dominate. The 79-foot Shivling rock formation at 4,800m is fully visible. The 5-day Parikrama circuit is open. This is the peak season for a reason: full accessibility, stable weather, and lower avalanche risk.

note: Peak continues. Warmest month. Highest trekking traffic. All routes fully open.
why_go: July is the warmest month of the season. Daytime temperatures at base (15–20°C) and at altitude (5–12°C) are comfortable. The Parikrama route is fully snow-free. Alpine wildflowers bloom. Visibility of the 6,055m peak and the Shivling formation is exceptional. This is the safest and most crowded window.

note: Late summer. Weather still stable. Trails drying out. Reduced crowds from July.
why_go: August is a secondary peak window. Weather remains stable; temperatures are warm (10–18°C daytime). The Parikrama route is fully accessible. Crowds drop compared to July. The trek is no less safe, just quieter. This is an excellent alternative to the July crunch.

note: Early autumn. Clear skies persist. Cooler but still trekking-friendly. Shoulder season.
who_should_avoid: Those uncomfortable with cooler nighttime temperatures
why_go: September brings autumn clarity. Skies remain clear. Daytime temperatures are mild (8–15°C); nights cool but not frigid. The Parikrama route is fully open and drying. Crowds are minimal. Views of Kinner Kailash and the Shivling are sharp. This is an excellent shoulder season.

note: Autumn ending. Early snow on high passes. Temperatures dropping. Season closing.
skip_reason: Early snow above 4,500m, temperature drop, rapid seasonal shift, reduced support.
why_not: October marks the close of the trekking season. Early snow falls on high passes above 4,500m. Daytime temperatures drop to 5–10°C; nights freeze (−5 to 0°C). The higher Parikrama route becomes risky. Infrastructure support (guides, lodges) begins reducing capacity. This is an unsafe window.

note: Winter onset. Snow accumulates. All high routes closed. Extreme conditions.
skip_reason: All high routes closed by snow, extreme cold (−10 to −15°C), no support infrastructure.
why_not: November brings winter. Heavy snow closes all trekking routes above 4,000m. Temperatures plummet to −10 to −15°C. The Parikrama route is completely impassable. Kalpa is accessible by road but remains very cold. This window is unsafe.

note: Deep winter. Complete snow closure. Extreme cold (−15 to −20°C). No access.
skip_reason: Complete snow closure, extreme cold, zero trekking infrastructure, avalanche hazard.
why_not: December is deep winter. All routes are buried under snow. Temperatures range from −15 to −20°C. Avalanche risk is extreme. No trekking is possible. This window is absolutely unsafe.

note: Winter. Deep snow on high passes. Manimahesh Lake frozen. Extreme cold.
skip_reason: Lake frozen, high passes snow-blocked, extreme cold (−15 to −20°C), zero support.
why_not: January is deep winter. Manimahesh Lake is frozen solid. The trek from Hadsar to Dhancho is blocked by snow above 3,500m. Temperatures drop to −15 to −20°C at altitude. No pilgrimage infrastructure is available. This window is categorically unsafe.

note: Winter deep. Lake frozen, passes closed. Coldest month with extreme conditions.
skip_reason: Frozen lake, complete snow closure, extreme cold (−20°C), avalanche risk.
why_not: February is the coldest month. Manimahesh Lake remains frozen. The trek is completely snow-blocked. Temperatures plummet to −20°C. No pilgrimage support exists. This window is unsafe.

note: Spring melt begins. Avalanche hazards peak. Passes unstable. Lake still frozen.
skip_reason: Avalanche risk from melt, pass instability, lake still frozen, minimal support.
why_not: March brings spring snow melt and high avalanche risk. Manimahesh Lake is still frozen. The trek route remains snow-clogged and unstable. Daytime temperatures at base warm to 5–10°C but nights are freezing. This window is unsafe.

note: Spring progression. Snow clearing but lake still frozen. Yatra does not begin until August.
skip_reason: Lake not yet unfrozen, yatra not yet scheduled, melt-hazards, early-season instability.
why_not: April sees lower-elevation snow clearing. However, Manimahesh Lake at 3,950m remains frozen. The official pilgrimage yatra does not begin until August (Janmashtami→Radha Ashtami). The trek is not yet operational. Visiting outside the yatra window goes against Gaddi tradition.

note: Late spring. Lake clearing but yatra still not scheduled. Early summer preparations underway.
skip_reason: Yatra not yet started, lake not fully thawed, support infrastructure not deployed.
why_not: May sees the lake beginning to thaw, but the official yatra does not begin until August. The pilgrimage window is specifically Janmashtami to Radha Ashtami (August–September). Infrastructure, guides, and lodges are not yet operational. This window is outside the sacred yatra season.

note: Early summer. Lake thawed but yatra not yet scheduled. Unofficial season.
skip_reason: Yatra not yet active, limited support, infrastructure not deployed.
why_not: June sees pleasant temperatures (10–18°C daytime) and a fully thawed lake. However, the official pilgrimage yatra has not begun. Infrastructure is minimal. Visiting outside the Janmashtami–Radha Ashtami window goes against Gaddi tribal tradition and misses the sacred yatra experience.

note: Pre-yatra season. Monsoon arriving. Infrastructure setup underway. Yatra begins next month.
skip_reason: Monsoon rains, yatra not yet started, infrastructure still being prepared.
why_not: July is pre-yatra season. The monsoon is arriving, bringing rains and potential landslides on the trek route. Infrastructure (guides, tents, food support) is being set up for August. Temperatures are mild (8–15°C) but moisture is high. The actual yatra begins on Janmashtami in early August.

note: Peak yatra season begins (Janmashtami→). Lake accessible. Full support infrastructure active.
who_should_avoid: Those with joint or knee issues
why_go: August is the heart of the yatra season. The pilgrimage begins on Janmashtami (Krishna's birthday). Manimahesh Lake is fully thawed and accessible for sacred bathing. Temperatures are cool (5–12°C daytime). The Gaddi shepherds and the local community are present and actively support pilgrims. The 7 km trek from Hadsar to Dhancho is moderate and well-maintained. This is the spiritually correct window.

note: Peak yatra continues (→Radha Ashtami). Stable weather. Prime pilgrimage window.
why_go: September is the culmination of the yatra season, ending on Radha Ashtami (Radha's birthday). Weather is exceptionally stable; daytime temperatures hover around 8–15°C. The lake is fully accessible and sacred. Thousands of pilgrims converge, creating a profound spiritual atmosphere. This is the entire reason for the yatra's existence.

note: Post-yatra season. Infrastructure dismantled. Early snow on high passes. Season closed.
skip_reason: Yatra ended, infrastructure withdrawn, early snow, reduced support.
why_not: October marks the close of the yatra season. Infrastructure is dismantled. Early snow falls on higher elevations above 4,500m. Daytime temperatures drop to 5–10°C; nights freeze. The Gaddi shepherds move down to lower elevations. Visiting outside the yatra window lacks spiritual purpose and community support.

note: Winter onset. Snow accumulates. Lake begins freezing. Extreme cold conditions.
skip_reason: Lake freezing, snow closure, extreme cold (−10 to −15°C), no support.
why_not: November brings winter. Manimahesh Lake begins freezing. Snow closes higher passes. Temperatures plummet to −10 to −15°C. The trek becomes unsafe. No infrastructure or community support exists. This window is unsafe.

note: Winter deep. Lake frozen solid. High passes snow-blocked. Extreme cold.
skip_reason: Lake frozen, complete snow closure, extreme cold (−15 to −20°C), zero access.
why_not: December is deep winter. Manimahesh Lake is frozen. All high passes are snow-blocked. Temperatures range from −15 to −20°C. The trek is completely inaccessible. This window is categorically unsafe.

note: Winter. Deep snow on all passes. Extreme cold. Glacier hazards at maximum.
skip_reason: All routes snow-blocked, extreme cold (−20 to −25°C), glacier crevasse danger.
why_not: January is severe winter. All trekking routes are buried under deep snow. The glaciers are treacherous. Temperatures plummet to −20 to −25°C. The trek is categorically unsafe. This window is absolutely prohibited.

note: Winter deep. Complete snow closure. Extreme cold persists. Avalanche risk.
skip_reason: Complete snow closure, extreme cold (−20°C), avalanche hazard at maximum.
why_not: February is the coldest month. All routes are completely snow-covered. Temperatures drop to −20°C or lower. Avalanche risk is extreme. The glaciers are unstable. This window is unsafe.

note: Spring melt begins. Avalanche hazards peak. Routes unstable. Still snow-blocked.
skip_reason: Avalanche risk from melt, pass instability, snow depth prohibitive, no access.
why_not: March brings spring melt and maximum avalanche danger on all high slopes. The trek routes remain snow-choked and unstable. Access is impossible. This window is unsafe.

note: Spring progression. Snow clearing from lower slopes. Higher passes still blocked.
skip_reason: High routes still snow-covered, late-season melt-hazard, yatra not yet scheduled.
why_not: April sees lower elevations clearing, but the core trek route above 4,000m remains heavily snow-covered. The official yatra does not begin until July (Shravan Purnima / full moon). Early access is unsafe and culturally inappropriate.

note: Late spring. Snow clearing at mid-elevations. High passes still impassable.
skip_reason: Upper trek still snow-covered, yatra not yet scheduled, summer not yet open.
why_not: May sees mid-elevation snow clearing. However, the higher glacial sections and passes above 4,500m remain heavily snow-covered. The yatra does not begin until July. Infrastructure is not deployed. This window is outside the sacred season.

note: Early summer. Lower snow, but upper glacier still blocked. Yatra prep underway.
skip_reason: Glacier sections still snow-blocked, yatra not yet active, official window begins next month.
why_not: June sees melting at lower elevations, but the glacial sections above 4,500m remain snowbound. The official yatra begins on Shravan Purnima (full moon in July–August). The trek is not yet safe. Infrastructure is being prepared but not yet active.

note: Peak yatra opens (Shravan Purnima full moon). Glaciers accessible. Full support active.
things_to_do: 32 km glacier and ice slope trekking
why_go: July opens the only trekking window, aligned with Shravan Purnima (full moon of Shravan month, sacred to Lord Shiva). The glaciers are sufficiently melted but still navigable. Temperatures at lower elevations are warm (12–18°C); at altitude (5,227m), frigid (−5 to 5°C). The 75-foot Shivalingam is accessible. Nain Sarovar lake is ice-free. This is the ONLY month the trek is possible.
festivals_this_month: Shravan Purnima (full moon; pilgrimage window opens)

note: Peak yatra continues into August. Slightly warmer. 80-degree ice slopes still hazardous.
why_go: August is the extension of the yatra window. Temperatures are slightly warmer than July (5–20°C at base; −2 to 8°C at altitude). However, this is still late in the yatra season. The 80-degree ice slopes remain technically challenging. Shravan month extends into early August, making this spiritually significant. This is a valid but technically harder window than July.

note: Post-yatra season. Glaciers refreezing. Early snow. Infrastructure dismantled.
skip_reason: Yatra ended, glaciers refreezing, early snow, reduced support, unsafe conditions.
why_not: September marks the end of the yatra season. Glaciers are refreezing after the summer melt, creating new crevasses and unstable surfaces. Early snow begins to accumulate at higher elevations. Infrastructure support is withdrawn. Daytime temperatures drop to 8–12°C; nights freeze. This window is unsafe.

note: Season closed. Snow accumulates on passes. Glaciers frozen and unstable. Extreme cold.
skip_reason: Glaciers frozen, heavy snow accumulation, extreme cold (−5 to −10°C), zero access.
why_not: October is autumn, and the trek is closed. Snow falls heavily on all passes above 4,500m. Glaciers are frozen and unstable. Crevasse danger is acute. Temperatures plummet to −5 to −10°C at altitude. The trek is not possible.

note: Early winter. Complete snow closure. Glaciers fully frozen. Extreme cold.
skip_reason: Complete snow closure, extreme cold (−10 to −15°C), glacier freeze, zero access.
why_not: November brings early winter. All passes and glacial sections are snowbound. Temperatures drop to −10 to −15°C. The glaciers are completely frozen and crevassed. No access is possible.

note: Deep winter. Severe snow cover. Extreme cold (−20°C). Completely inaccessible.
skip_reason: Deep snow closure, extreme cold (−20°C), glacier freeze, crevasse hazard.
why_not: December is deep winter. All routes are buried under severe snow. Temperatures drop to −20°C or lower. Glaciers are completely frozen and crevassed. The trek is absolutely unsafe and categorically prohibited.
